parties.name: Communist Party of Ukraine
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Communist Party of Ukraine, the republican branch of the CPSU with more than two million members, holds a monopoly of power in the Ukrainian SSR. Its First Secretary since 1963 is Petro Shelest, a full member of the Politburo in Moscow, while his rival Volodymyr Shcherbytsky heads the republic's Council of Ministers. The party governs 47 million people, the Donbas coalfields, the Dnieper steelworks and the Union's breadbasket.

Shelest combines orthodoxy with Ukrainian assertiveness: he pressed for the invasion of Czechoslovakia, yet defends the republic's industry against Moscow's ministries, encourages Ukrainian language and history and protects the cultural elite more than his rivals like. The party's leverage is total within the republic, though Brezhnev's Dnipropetrovsk allies are waiting for Shelest to stumble.
parties.economic_identity: State socialism built around coal, steel, machinery, and grain, with a choice between Union-scale heavy industry and republican consumer reinvestment.

parties.name: Ukrainian Supreme Liberation Council
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Ukrainian Supreme Liberation Council was founded in the Carpathians in 1944 as the political authority of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army. Since the insurgency was crushed it survives through its Foreign Representation in New York, led by Mykola Lebed, wartime acting chief of the Bandera wing, and the priest Ivan Hrynioch. Their Prolog publishing house and the Munich monthly Suchasnist, quietly funded by American intelligence, reach Soviet visitors and intellectuals.

The council claims to be the rightful underground authority of an independent Ukraine and works hand in hand with Washington against Moscow. It has shed the one-party creed of integral nationalism for a pragmatic Western course, yet remains a tight conspiracy whose leaders expect to rule by right of the liberation struggle. Its leverage is American money and émigré scholarship.
parties.economic_identity: Anti-Soviet national liberation with civilian oversight, diaspora-supported education, and a negotiated transition from underground authority.

parties.name: State Centre of the Ukrainian People's Republic in Exile
parties.registered_name: Derzhavnyi Tsentr Ukrayinskoyi Narodnoyi Respubliky v ekzyli
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The State Centre of the Ukrainian People's Republic in Exile carries the legal continuity of the republic that Symon Petliura defended until 1920. Its President since 1967 is Mykola Livytsky, son of the earlier exile president Andriy Livytsky, who presides from Munich over an exile government and the Ukrainian National Council, a parliament of émigré parties from Germany, North America and Australia.

It stands for an independent, democratic and Christian Ukraine, a parliamentary republic with private property and a market economy, firmly in the Western camp. It lobbies governments abroad, commemorates the national revolution and the famine of 1933, and rejects both Soviet rule and the authoritarian nationalism of the Bandera wing. Its leverage is legitimacy and the votes of Ukrainian communities in Canada and the United States.
parties.economic_identity: Parliamentary national democracy with a social-market economy, agrarian reform, and coalition government across exile parties.

parties.name: The Sixtiers
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
The Sixtiers are the generation of Ukrainian poets, critics and artists who came of age in the Khrushchev thaw and refused to accept Russification. After the arrests of 1965 and 1966 they turned to samizdat and open letters. The journalist Vyacheslav Chornovil, whose record of the political trials circulated abroad as The Chornovil Papers, the critic Ivan Svitlychny and the painter Alla Horska are their leading figures in Lviv and Kyiv.

They demand that the Soviet constitution be honoured: free speech, open trials, an end to political imprisonment and equal standing for Ukrainian in schools, universities and publishing. Democratic and humanist rather than revolutionary, they look to European culture and the Moscow rights defenders. Their leverage lies in moral authority, samizdat, Western radio and the sympathy of students.
parties.economic_identity: Civic liberalism rooted in Ukrainian language, legal rights, universities, and small enterprise rather than a ready-made nationalist party.

parties.name: Ukrainian Revolutionary Democratic Party
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Ukrainian Revolutionary Democratic Party is the left-of-centre party of the post-war emigration, founded in the displaced persons' camps of Germany by the novelist Ivan Bahrianyi, a Soviet camp survivor who refused to go home. Since Bahrianyi's death in 1963 his collaborators have led it around the weekly Ukrainski Visti in Neu-Ulm, giving former Soviet citizens from eastern Ukraine a voice in the Ukrainian National Council.

It stands for an independent, democratic Ukraine with a social market economy, land for those who work it, strong unions and a welfare state, combining anti-communism with respect for the social gains of the revolution. It rejects the authoritarian nationalism of the Bandera wing and seeks partners among Western social democrats. Its leverage is modest: its press and its seats in the exile parliament.
parties.economic_identity: Democratic socialism with cooperative land reform, independent labour, public services, and a market economy restrained by parliamentary law.

parties.name: Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (Melnyk)
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Melnyk wing of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists descends from the movement's founding leadership under Yevhen Konovalets and his successor Colonel Andriy Melnyk, who died in Luxembourg in 1964. Now led by Oleh Shtul-Zhdanovych from Paris, it is the more moderate of the émigré nationalist camps, strong among intellectuals, veterans and cultural societies in France, Belgium and North America, and part of the exile institutions of the Ukrainian People's Republic.

It preaches disciplined national solidarity: an independent, Christian and socially conservative Ukraine built on family, village and cooperatives, strong leadership and popular mobilisation against Russification. Firmly anti-communist and Western-leaning, it rejects the violent methods of the Bandera wing. Its leverage lies in its press, its scholars and memories of the 1930s nationalist movement among older Galicians.
parties.economic_identity: Christian conservative nationalism, national cooperatives, disciplined public service, and coalition with non-revolutionary exile institutions.

parties.name: Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (Bandera)
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Bandera wing of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists is the largest and most militant of the émigré camps, heir to the wartime insurgency in western Ukraine. After a KGB assassin killed Stepan Bandera in Munich in 1959, leadership passed in 1968 to Yaroslav Stetsko, who proclaimed Ukrainian statehood in Lviv in 1941 and heads the Anti-Bolshevik Bloc of Nations, a member of the World Anti-Communist League.

It holds to the integral nationalism of Dmytro Dontsov: the nation above all, a disciplined revolutionary order and a single national movement ruling an independent Ukraine won by revolution and the break-up of the Soviet empire. Fiercely anti-Russian, it courts Western conservatives while scorning liberal democracy. Its leverage lies in its Munich headquarters, youth organizations and veterans of the insurgency.
parties.economic_identity: Authoritarian anti-communist nationalism, centralized political command, and state-directed industrial mobilization at the cost of pluralist legitimacy.

nodes.title: Republican Mandate
nodes.description: Our republic stands between the ambitions of its people and the demands of a continental Union. The republican administration must turn ministries, local councils and industrial managers into a government capable of securing investment and delivering what it promises.

nodes.title: Union Appointments
nodes.description: Officials with experience in the Union ministries know where allocations are decided and which signatures open doors. Bringing them into our administration will strengthen those connections, although republican priorities may receive less generous consideration when the centre issues its instructions.

nodes.title: Republican Cadres
nodes.description: Administrators who know our towns, farms and factories can see difficulties that disappear in distant reports. Promoting them will give republican institutions deeper roots, while obliging us to accommodate influential local networks and their expectations.

nodes.title: Cadre Schools

nodes.title: Professional Audits

nodes.title: Cadre Discipline
nodes.description: Warnings and quiet transfers have allowed too many officials to mistake their positions for private property. A concentrated disciplinary campaign will replace compromised administrators and reassert central authority, even if the upheaval briefly unsettles factories and local institutions.
runtime_contract: IMP_is_1970_scenario and COLDWAR_SOV_is_union_republic and a recorded scenario SSR identity or a subsequently accepted SSR admission. A whitelisted puppet by itself is insufficient.

runtime_contract: IMP_is_1970_scenario and COLDWAR_SOV_is_union_republic and a recorded scenario SSR identity or a subsequently accepted SSR admission. A whitelisted puppet by itself is insufficient.

nodes.title: Plan Negotiations

nodes.title: Union Priorities
nodes.description: The Union's strategic programmes offer large and dependable orders to enterprises willing to meet demanding specifications. nodes.title: Local Reinvestment

nodes.title: Secretariat School

nodes.title: Controlled Debate

nodes.title: A Unified Line

nodes.title: Republican Statute

nodes.title: Republican Delegation

nodes.title: Republican Accounts
nodes.description: Reports assembled to satisfy production targets do not always reveal the condition of an economy. A republican survey of deliveries, employment and enterprise accounts will expose the shortages hidden behind impressive totals and give future investment a firmer basis.

nodes.title: Industrial Combines

nodes.title: Consumer Supply
nodes.description: Households judge economic progress by the goods they can obtain rather than the tonnage reported by heavy industry. Expanding consumer supply and distribution will answer those expectations, drawing investment away from military production and larger industrial monuments.

nodes.title: Enterprise Accounts
nodes.description: Enterprises need to know what their inputs cost and whether their customers can use the goods they deliver. Revised accounting will reward usable production and expose chronic losses, while retaining the wider economic obligations of the republican plan.

nodes.title: Output Incentives

nodes.title: Quality Contracts

nodes.title: Freight Connections

nodes.title: Food Processing

nodes.title: Machine Tools

nodes.title: Distribution Network

nodes.title: Power Investment

nodes.title: Energy Discipline

nodes.title: Maintenance Stocks

nodes.title: Diversify Orders

parties.name: Communist Party of Byelorussia
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Communist Party of Byelorussia, the republican branch of the CPSU, holds a monopoly of power in the Byelorussian SSR. Its First Secretary since 1965 is Pyotr Masherov, a former schoolteacher, partisan commander and Hero of the Soviet Union, perhaps the most popular republican leader in the Union, while Cichan Kisialioŭ heads the government. The party rules a republic rebuilt from a war that killed a quarter of its people.

Masherov pairs loyalty to Moscow with energetic modernization: tractor and truck plants in Minsk, potash at Salihorsk, oil refining at Navapolatsk and the draining of the Palesse marshes. He cultivates the partisan legend, opened the Khatyn memorial in 1969, promotes Russian as the language of progress and keeps nationalism firmly down. Its leverage is total within the republic.
parties.economic_identity: Public machine-building and chemical production supported by eastern trade, with a choice between export specialization and household supply.

parties.name: Rada of the Belarusian Democratic Republic
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Rada of the Belarusian Democratic Republic is the oldest government-in-exile in the world, the council that proclaimed Belarusian independence on 25 March 1918 before the Bolsheviks took Minsk. Its president, Mikoła Abramčyk, leads it from Paris, assisted by Vincent Žuk-Hryškievič in Canada, and every 25 March its supporters across the diaspora celebrate Independence Day.

The Rada stands for an independent, democratic and parliamentary Belarus within its ethnographic borders, with private property, religious freedom for Orthodox and Catholics alike and a place in the Western community of nations. It condemns both Soviet rule and the wartime collaboration of its rival, the Belarusian Central Council. Its leverage is legitimacy, the Belarusian-American Association and the sympathy of Western governments.
parties.economic_identity: Exile constitutional continuity, democratic representation, Belarusian-language renewal, and a negotiated market transition.

parties.name: The Hrodna Circle
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
The Hrodna Circle gathers the liberal Belarusian intelligentsia around the writer Vasil Bykaŭ, a frontline officer whose stark war novellas, above all The Dead Feel No Pain, printed in Novy Mir in 1966, were savaged by the party press for slandering the Soviet soldier. Bykaŭ lives in Hrodna alongside his friend Aleksiej Karpiuk, a writer and former partisan, and their readers include young poets, historians and teachers who refuse official lies.

They want honesty about the war and Stalin's crimes, freedom for the press and creative work, legality and dignity for the Belarusian language in schools and public life. They admire Tvardovsky's Novy Mir and the Moscow rights defenders and look to European humanism rather than to any bloc. Their leverage is literary prestige and readers across the Union.
parties.economic_identity: Municipal pluralism, bilingual services, local enterprise, and cultural preservation through schools and libraries.

parties.name: The Minsk Spring
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
The Minsk Spring is the reform-communist mood of Belarusian academics, editors and younger officials who hoped the Prague Spring would give socialism a human face. Its leading figure is the writer and literary scholar Aleś Adamovič, a teenage partisan who was forced out of Moscow University in 1966 for refusing to condemn the writers Sinyavsky and Daniel and now works at the Academy's Institute of Literature in Minsk.

They want democratic socialism rather than capitalism: accountable soviets, a free press, independent courts, enterprise self-management and the truth about collectivization, the purges and the war. They see Western social democrats and Italian communists as partners and detente as an opportunity. Their leverage lies in the universities, the Academy and young officials impatient with Brezhnev's caution.
parties.economic_identity: Reform socialism with cultural autonomy, public services, enterprise accounting, and an orderly opening to small business.

profile.name: Moldavian SSR
profile.context: Food processing, agriculture and cross-Dniester industry

regional.name: Uneven Processing Networks
regional.description: The republic's established economy rests on food processing, agriculture and cross-dniester industry. These strengths bring inherited costs in transport, public administration and the inputs needed to keep production operating reliably.

parties.name: Communist Party of Moldavia
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Communist Party of Moldavia is the republican branch of the CPSU and the sole legal party in the Moldavian SSR. Since 1961 it has been led by First Secretary Ivan Bodiul, a loyal protégé of Leonid Brezhnev, who governs through a cadre corps dominated by Russians, Ukrainians and Russified Moldavians.

The party upholds the doctrine of a Moldavian nation distinct from the Romanians, the Cyrillic script and the steady Russification of public life. Its economic priority is agro-industrial specialisation: vineyards, orchards, tobacco and canning on a massive scale. Its power rests on the nomenklatura, control of every institution and the protection of Brezhnev's Moldavian network in Moscow.
parties.economic_identity: State ownership anchored in wine, food processing, agricultural machinery, and cross-Dniester industrial trade.

parties.name: National Peasants' Party
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The National Peasants' Party was interwar Romania's great agrarian-democratic force and drew Bessarabia's peasant movement into its ranks in the 1920s. Banned by the communists in 1947, it survives only through exile committees in Paris, London and New York and through aged veterans at home, among them the Bessarabian tribune Pantelimon Halippa, now living quietly in Bucharest.

Its programme combines Christian-democratic values, private smallholdings and parliamentary rule with firm anti-Sovietism. For Moldavian villagers forced into kolkhozes and for survivors of the 1949 deportations, its memory stands for land, church and Romanian unity. Organised activity in the republic is impossible; its leverage lies in rural memory and émigré networks.
parties.economic_identity: Agrarian democracy, family ownership, rural credit, and gradual reform of collective farms with compensation for displaced claimants.

parties.name: Writers' Union of the Moldavian SSR
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
The Writers' Union of the Moldavian SSR is the official guild of the republic's authors, yet during the 1960s it became the main shelter for cautious cultural liberalisation. Prose writer Ion Druţă and poet Grigore Vieru embody a generation that writes about village life, the native tongue and historical memory, drawing repeated rebukes from First Secretary Ivan Bodiul's ideologists.

The writers seek greater freedom of expression, respect for the Moldavian language and its unity with Romanian letters, and an end to crude Russification. They do not challenge Soviet power openly, but their journals, readings and loyal readership give them a moral authority that no other legal body in the republic possesses.
parties.economic_identity: Cultural self-government, public education, multilingual civic rights, and food-sector modernization under a negotiated social market.

parties.name: Socialism with a Human Face
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
Socialism with a Human Face is the loose milieu of younger economists, teachers and party members in Chişinău who followed the Prague Spring with sympathy in 1968. Since the Warsaw Pact intervention they keep silent at party meetings, but quietly pass around Czech and Yugoslav reform literature and Romanian press reports critical of the invasion.

They favour economic decentralisation, enterprise self-management, open debate within the party and an end to censorship, while remaining loyal to socialism and preferring a reformed Union to secession. Their strength lies in the university, research institutes and the Academy of Sciences; their weakness is the vigilance of the KGB and Bodiul's apparatus.
parties.economic_identity: Reform socialism with public ownership, enterprise autonomy, workers' voice, and civil liberties for a multilingual society.

parties.name: National Patriotic Front
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The National Patriotic Front is a secret organisation formed at the end of the 1960s by young Chişinău intellectuals, among them Alexandru Usatiuc-Bulgăr, Gheorghe Ghimpu and Valeriu Graur. Working in strict conspiracy, it recruits teachers, engineers and students who reject the official doctrine of a separate Moldavian nation.

Its programme calls for a Moldavian Democratic Republic, secession from the USSR and union with Romania, together with the Latin script and the teaching of Romanian national history. Its members hope for help from Bucharest and Western radio. Numerically tiny and hunted by the KGB, it draws its leverage from a widespread, unspoken national resentment that it aims to turn into a movement.
parties.economic_identity: Anti-Soviet national independence, Romanian-language institutions, rural property reform, and a distinct diplomatic settlement with Romania.

parties.name: Communist Party of Estonia
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Communist Party of Estonia is the republican branch of the CPSU and the sole legal party of the Estonian SSR. Founded in 1920, it was driven underground after its failed Tallinn uprising of December 1924, installed in power by the Soviet annexation of 1940 and purged in 1950 of its 'bourgeois nationalists'. Since then it has been led by First Secretary Johannes Käbin, an Estonian raised in Russia.

Käbin combines strict loyalty to Moscow with a quiet Estonianisation of the cadres and a degree of economic and cultural latitude that makes the republic the Soviet Union's showcase 'West'. The party controls every ministry, enterprise, newspaper and collective farm and relies on the KGB and the Baltic Military District, while bargaining with Moscow for investment.
parties.economic_identity: Public engineering and oil-shale industry balanced against cleaner energy use, Baltic trade, and consumer production.

parties.name: Estonian Government in Exile
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Estonian Government in Exile claims unbroken continuity with the Republic overrun in 1940. It descends from the cabinet of Otto Tief, appointed in September 1944 by Jüri Uluots as Prime Minister in duties of the President, shortly before Uluots and several ministers escaped to Sweden. Since 1963 the veteran diplomat Aleksander Warma has held that office in Stockholm, with Tõnis Kint serving as acting Prime Minister.

It rests its legitimacy on the 1938 constitution of Konstantin Päts's presidential order and on the Western policy of non-recognition of the annexation. Implacably anti-Soviet and aligned with the United States, it has no territory, army or formal recognition, yet it remains the legal symbol around which exile lobbying, radio broadcasts to the homeland and hopes of restoration revolve.
parties.economic_identity: Restored parliamentary sovereignty, legal continuity, broad citizenship, and a gradual return to private and cooperative enterprise.

parties.name: Estonian National Council
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Estonian National Council was founded in Stockholm in 1947 as the representative assembly of the tens of thousands of Estonians who crossed the Baltic to Sweden in 1944. Drawing its members from exile societies, veterans' associations and former politicians of the Republic, it acts as a quasi-parliament for the exile community and as the political backbone of the government in exile.

Its outlook is national-conservative: restoration of the Republic as it stood in 1940, unconditional rejection of the Soviet annexation and no cultural traffic with Soviet Estonia that might lend the regime legitimacy. It lobbies Swedish and American politicians, remembers the 1946 extradition of Baltic soldiers from Sweden and supports Estonian schools and choirs abroad. Its leverage lies in organisation and moral authority.
parties.economic_identity: Broad exile coalition, pluralist parliamentary rule, cultural education, and mixed public-private reconstruction.

parties.name: The Cassette Generation
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
The Cassette Generation takes its name from the boxed sets of slim debut collections in which the state publishing house introduced young Estonian poets from 1962. Paul-Eerik Rummo, Jaan Kaplinski, Viivi Luik and their peers grew up after the war, read Western modernists and Finnish poets, and turned Estonian verse away from socialist realism toward irony, nature and private conscience.

They are no organisation, but they are the voice of the liberal intelligentsia: freedom of expression, open contacts with Finland and the West, respect for the Estonian language and an honest reckoning with the past. Since the crushing of the Prague Spring the censors cut their lines more sharply, yet their readings fill halls in Tartu and Tallinn Their leverage is the prestige of the written word.
parties.economic_identity: Cultural self-government, university autonomy, environmental standards, and a gradual opening for small technical firms.

parties.name: Estonian Socialist Party
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Estonian Socialist Party is the exile continuation of the Estonian Socialist Workers' Party, the inter-war home of Estonian social democracy and the party of August Rei, State Elder in 1928-29 and head of the government in exile until his death in 1963. Re-established among the refugees in Sweden, it belongs to the Socialist International through the Socialist Union of Central-Eastern Europe.

It stands for a restored democratic Estonia with a Nordic-style welfare state, free trade unions and close ties to Sweden and Finland. It rejects Soviet rule as a perversion of socialism and works with Swedish, British and German social democrats to keep the Baltic question alive in the International. Its base is ageing exile workers, teachers and intellectuals in Stockholm, Toronto and New York.
parties.economic_identity: Exile social democracy, collective bargaining, universal services, and a mixed industrial economy with strong public standards.

parties.name: Communist Party of Latvia
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Communist Party of Latvia is the republican branch of the CPSU and the only legal party of the Latvian SSR. Underground throughout independence and decimated by Stalin's purges of Latvian Bolsheviks in Moscow, it was installed in power by the annexation of 1940. Since 1966 it has been led by First Secretary Augusts Voss, a Siberian-born Latvian and protégé of his predecessor Arvīds Pelše.

Under Voss the party keeps the strict line set after the 1959 purge of national communists: Russian as the working language of the apparatus, rapid growth of all-Union industry and a mass inflow of labour from Russia, Ukraine and Belarus into Riga. It controls every lever of power, but its increasingly Russian-speaking cadres leave it estranged from much of the Latvian nation.
parties.economic_identity: Public engineering and port industry balanced against consumer services, local supplier networks, and export dependence.

parties.name: Latvian Diplomatic Service
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Latvian Diplomatic Service is the last functioning organ of the independent Republic. On 17 May 1940, a month before the Soviet invasion, Kārlis Ulmanis's cabinet secretly granted emergency powers to the envoy in London, Kārlis Zariņš, to head all Latvian missions abroad. Since Zariņš's death in 1963 the historian-diplomat Arnolds Spekke has led the service from the legation in Washington, with Anatols Dinbergs at his side.

It embodies the legal continuity of the state as it stood under Ulmanis's authoritarian presidency: non-recognition of the annexation, custody of Latvian assets abroad and passports for exiles. Firmly aligned with Washington and London, it stands aloof from émigré party quarrels. Its leverage is legal and symbolic, resting entirely on the Western policy of non-recognition.
parties.economic_identity: State continuity, constitutional diplomacy, inclusive citizenship, and investment paced to the return of skilled residents.

parties.name: World Federation of Free Latvians
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The World Federation of Free Latvians was founded in 1955 as the umbrella of the Latvian national associations in the United States, Canada, Australia and Western Europe, which unite the refugees who fled the Red Army in 1944-45. It coordinates Latvian schools, churches, newspapers and the great exile song festivals, and it lobbies Western governments to uphold non-recognition of the Soviet annexation.

Its outlook is national-conservative and staunchly anti-communist: restoration of an independent Latvia, rejection of cultural exchanges that might legitimise the Soviet regime and preservation of Latvian identity among the young born abroad. It works closely with the diplomatic service and with American Captive Nations groups. Its leverage lies in money, organisation and access to legislators in Washington, Ottawa and Canberra.
parties.economic_identity: Diaspora coalition, democratic restoration, language schooling, and private investment under parliamentary oversight.

parties.name: The Sixtiers
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
The Sixtiers are the poets who came of age during the Thaw and transformed Latvian literature in the 1960s. Ojārs Vācietis, Imants Ziedonis and Vizma Belševica write in a personal, ironic and often bitter voice. Belševica's 1969 collection 'Gadu gredzeni', whose cycle of Henry of Livonia's notes in the margins of his chronicle of the German conquest reads as an allegory of occupation, brought an official campaign against her and a ban on publication.

They have no organisation, but they speak for the liberal intelligentsia: freedom of expression, honest history, the dignity of the Latvian language and an end to the dogmas of socialist realism. Not separatists, they are nonetheless read for national meanings between every line. Their leverage lies in the immense prestige of poetry in Latvian society.
parties.economic_identity: Civic cultural renewal, bilingual public access, local enterprise, and environmental reform of industrial production.

parties.name: Latvian Social Democratic Workers' Party
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Latvian Social Democratic Workers' Party, founded in 1904, was the largest party in the Saeima of independent Latvia until Kārlis Ulmanis dissolved parliament and banned all parties in his coup of May 1934. Its leaders were jailed first by Ulmanis and then by the Soviets; survivors re-formed it in exile, where it belongs to the Socialist International and is led from Stockholm by Bruno Kalniņš, son of the last Saeima speaker Pauls Kalniņš.

It stands for a restored parliamentary democracy with a Nordic welfare state, strong unions and friendship with Sweden. It condemns both Ulmanis's dictatorship and Soviet rule and remains wary of the nationalist right that dominates exile institutions. Its leverage lies in its ties to Swedish, British and German social democrats.

parties.name: Communist Party of Lithuania
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Communist Party of Lithuania is the republican branch of the CPSU and the only legal party of the Lithuanian SSR. Founded in 1918 and illegal throughout independence, it was carried to power by the Soviet annexation of 1940 and led through the war against the partisans by Antanas Sniečkus, its First Secretary since 1936 and now among the Union's longest-serving party chiefs.

Sniečkus pairs unwavering loyalty to Moscow with a careful defence of Lithuanian interests: native cadres in leading posts, restrained immigration, new industry spread to provincial towns rather than concentrated in Vilnius, and measured tolerance for national culture. Under him a small underground sect has become a mass party of Lithuanians. It controls every institution of the republic.
parties.economic_identity: Public manufacturing and food production with republican cadre autonomy and a durable social settlement with Catholic communities.

parties.name: Lithuanian Diplomatic Service
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Lithuanian Diplomatic Service is the surviving apparatus of the pre-war Republic. In June 1940, on the eve of the Soviet occupation, the Lithuanian government secretly named Stasys Lozoraitis, envoy in Rome and Antanas Smetona's former foreign minister, Chief of the Diplomatic Service. Lozoraitis has led it from Rome ever since, with legations in Washington and London that Western governments still recognise.

It embodies the legal continuity of the Smetona-era state: non-recognition of the annexation, custody of Lithuanian assets abroad and passports for exiles. Pro-Western and conservative, it claims to stand above émigré parties, which has fuelled a long rivalry with the Supreme Committee for the Liberation of Lithuania over who speaks for the nation. Its leverage is legal and diplomatic, resting on Washington's policy of non-recognition.
parties.economic_identity: Legal restoration with inclusive civic citizenship, parliamentary oversight, land claims, and a staged return of private enterprise.

parties.name: Lithuanian Christian Democratic Party
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Lithuanian Christian Democratic Party was the strongest party of the parliamentary republic in the 1920s; it briefly backed Antanas Smetona's 1926 coup before being pushed into opposition and banned in 1936. In exile it is the leading force in the Supreme Committee for the Liberation of Lithuania, and its patriarch is the priest Mykolas Krupavičius, architect of the land reform and the committee's chairman from 1945 to 1955, now living in Chicago.

It stands for a restored democratic Lithuania built on Catholic social teaching: the family, private property tempered by social justice, Catholic schooling and ties to the Holy See. It distrusts both the Smetona nationalists and the liberals who seek contacts with Soviet Lithuania. Its leverage lies in the parishes, press and associations of Lithuanian America.
parties.economic_identity: Catholic social market, parish education, cooperative ownership, family farms, and civic welfare under elected government.

parties.name: Santara-Šviesa Federation
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
Santara-Šviesa is the federation of liberal Lithuanian exile intellectuals formed in 1957 by the merger of two student movements born in the post-war refugee years. Its leading mind is the sociologist Vytautas Kavolis, editor of the journal Metmenys, and its annual summer conferences in the American Midwest draw scholars, writers and young professionals raised in exile.

It stands for liberal democracy, pluralism, secular culture and an open, critical debate on Lithuanian history, including the uncomfortable chapters of 1941. Unlike most exile bodies it favours cautious cultural contacts with Soviet Lithuania as a bridge to the people at home, which earns it charges of naivety from the Catholic and nationalist establishment. Its leverage lies in ideas, in American universities and in the younger generation of the emigration.
parties.economic_identity: Liberal cultural renewal, civil liberties, university autonomy, and small enterprise connected to diaspora knowledge.

parties.name: Social Democratic Party of Lithuania
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Social Democratic Party of Lithuania, founded in 1896, is the oldest Lithuanian political party. A partner in the 1926 coalition overthrown by Smetona's coup and banned with the other parties in 1936, it reconstituted itself in exile, where it sits in the Supreme Committee for the Liberation of Lithuania and belongs to the Socialist International. Its long-time leader Steponas Kairys, a signatory of the 1918 Act of Independence, died in New York in 1964.

It stands for a restored parliamentary democracy with a welfare state, trade-union rights and secular education. It rejects Soviet rule as a perversion of socialism and works with Western social democrats to keep Baltic independence on the agenda. Its base is ageing pre-war activists in America and Western Europe.
parties.economic_identity: Parliamentary social democracy, organized labour, cooperative agriculture, and public ownership of essential services.

parties.name: Lithuanian Nationalist Union
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Lithuanian Nationalist Union, the tautininkai, was the ruling party of Antanas Smetona's authoritarian regime from the coup of December 1926 to the Soviet occupation of 1940, and the only party permitted after 1936. Smetona died in exile in Cleveland in 1944, and his followers keep the movement alive in the United States through their own national league and the Cleveland weekly Dirva.

It stands for an integral nationalism built around the nation and a strong leader: discipline, patriotism, reverence for Smetona as 'Leader of the Nation' and suspicion of party politics. It rejects all contact with Soviet Lithuania and contests the Christian Democrats' dominance of exile institutions. Its leverage lies in veterans of the pre-war state apparatus and in a press that still shapes conservative émigré opinion.
parties.economic_identity: Conservative national development, centralized executive authority, domestic enterprise, and cultural institutions under state supervision.

parties.name: Communist Party of Georgia
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Communist Party of Georgia is the republican branch of the CPSU and the only legal party in the Georgian SSR. Since 1953 it has been led by First Secretary Vasil Mzhavanadze, a former army general and candidate member of the Politburo, who governs through an easy-going system of patronage that keeps the republic calm and prosperous by Soviet standards.

The party balances loyalty to Moscow with tolerance for Georgian pride, a thriving second economy and rampant corruption that reaches into Mzhavanadze's own household. It promotes tea, citrus, wine, tourism and heavy industry in Rustavi and Kutaisi. Its power rests on the nomenklatura and on Brezhnev's goodwill, which ambitious rivals are already testing.
parties.economic_identity: Public light industry, wine and tea processing, Black Sea commerce, and negotiated regional development.

parties.name: Writers' Union of Georgia
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
The Writers' Union of Georgia is the official guild of the republic's authors and guardian of a literary tradition reaching back to Shota Rustaveli. Its ranks span the elder novelist Konstantine Gamsakhurdia, the popular prose writer Nodar Dumbadze and a younger generation of poets who treat the Georgian language almost as a sacred trust.

Loyal to Soviet power in public, the union defends the primacy of Georgian in schools and administration, the protection of churches and monuments, and a proud national history. It resists Russification and centralisation with petitions and quiet lobbying. Its leverage lies in the immense prestige of literature in Georgian society and the party's fear of offending national pride.
parties.economic_identity: Cultural civic nationalism, Georgian-language education, regional accommodation, and support for publishing and tourism.

parties.name: Union of Cinematographers of Georgia
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
The Union of Cinematographers of Georgia brings together the directors of the Georgia-Film studio, whose work has made Georgian cinema famous across the Soviet Union and at Western festivals. Tengiz Abuladze, Otar Iosseliani, Eldar and Giorgi Shengelaia and Lana Gogoberidze belong to a generation that prizes irony, poetry and individual conscience over socialist realism.

Their films test the censors with ambiguity and humour, and some, like Iosseliani's, run into trouble with Goskino. They want artistic freedom, contacts with Europe and an honest look at Georgian life, without challenging Soviet power head-on. Their leverage lies in an international prestige that Moscow is reluctant to sacrifice.
parties.economic_identity: Cultural industry, technical education, tourism, and municipal investment rather than a state built around one capital's studios.

parties.name: Social Democratic Party of Georgia
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Social Democratic Party of Georgia, the Menshevik party that governed the independent Democratic Republic of Georgia from 1918 until the Red Army invasion of 1921, survives in French exile. Its centre is the estate at Leuville-sur-Orge near Paris, where Noe Zhordania's government-in-exile sat until his death in 1953 and where the émigré community still gathers.

The party stands for democratic socialism, parliamentary government, land for the peasants and an independent Georgia within a free Europe, and keeps ties with European social democrats. Its veterans are ageing and their children assimilating. Inside Georgia its legacy is officially reviled, but family memories of 1918 keep its name alive.
parties.economic_identity: Pluralist social democracy, cooperative agriculture, elected local government, labour rights, and gradual industrial modernization.

parties.name: Communist Party of Armenia
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Communist Party of Armenia, founded in 1920 and a republican branch of the CPSU, holds a monopoly of power in the Armenian SSR. Its First Secretary since February 1966 is Anton Kochinyan, the long-serving former premier installed after Moscow removed Yakov Zarobyan, whose tolerance of the national mood around the 1965 genocide anniversary had alarmed the Kremlin. Badal Muradyan heads the Council of Ministers and Nagush Harutyunyan the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet.

The party governs a small, fast-industrialising republic of 2.5 million people, building chemical works, power stations and electronics plants while sanctioning memorials such as Tsitsernakaberd and Sardarapat to channel national feeling. Kochinyan's line is loyalty to Brezhnev, cautious patronage of Armenian culture and firm suppression of open nationalism. Its leverage is total: the nomenklatura, the press, the courts and the security organs all answer to its Central Committee.
parties.economic_identity: Public engineering, scientific education, local supplier development, and balanced investment in power and workshops.

parties.name: Armenian Revolutionary Federation
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Dashnaktsutyun, founded in Tiflis in 1890, governed the independent Republic of Armenia in 1918-1920 and has been outlawed on Soviet soil since the Bolsheviks took Yerevan. On 1 January 1970 it is the strongest organisation of the Armenian diaspora, directed by a Bureau in Beirut, with mass bases in Lebanon, Syria, Iran, France and the United States, the newspapers Aztag and Hairenik and the Armenian Youth Federation.

Its programme remains a free, independent and united Armenia including the provinces held by Turkey, and it treats Soviet rule as occupation. In the Cold War this has made it a partner of the West: it backed Camille Chamoun in Lebanon's 1958 crisis and stands behind the Catholicosate of Cilicia in Antelias against Etchmiadzin. Its leverage is money, discipline and a dense web of schools, clubs and scouts that keeps the exiles hostile to Moscow.
parties.economic_identity: Socialist-national independence, diaspora-supported development, public education, and a strong but contested national mandate.

parties.name: Armenian Democratic Liberal Party
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Ramgavar Party was formed in Constantinople in 1921 by the merger of the Armenakan Party, the Reformed Hnchaks and the Armenian Constitutional Democrats. Banned in Soviet Armenia, it lives in the communities of Beirut, Cairo, Aleppo, Boston and Paris, where its merchants, doctors and lawyers publish Zartonk and Baikar and sit on the boards of the Armenian General Benevolent Union.

Its creed is bourgeois liberalism wrapped in patriotism: private property, parliamentary politics, respect for the Church and loyalty to the existing Armenian homeland whatever its regime. Since the 1940s it has backed repatriation and cultural ties with Soviet Armenia and sided with Etchmiadzin against the Dashnaks, while its members vote for Western parties at home. Inside the republic its appeal lies with families that have relatives abroad and with a respectable, church-going middle class.
parties.economic_identity: Diaspora liberalism, private and cooperative enterprise, university autonomy, and accommodation between homeland and overseas communities.

parties.name: Social Democrat Hunchakian Party
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
Founded in Geneva in 1887 by Armenian students around Avetis Nazarbekian, the Hnchak party was the first socialist party in the Ottoman and Persian lands. Never a governing force, it survived the genocide and the Soviet takeover in the diaspora, where it is active in Beirut, Aleppo, Cairo and the United States with its own clubs, schools and newspapers.

Since the 1920s the Hnchaks have regarded Soviet Armenia as the realised homeland and defend it against the Dashnaks, while keeping their own Marxist but non-Leninist social-democratic identity. They call for social justice, welfare for workers and refugees, recognition of the genocide and the recovery of lost lands through Soviet power. Their leverage lies among the diaspora's working poor and in their usefulness to Moscow as friendly socialists outside the CPSU.
parties.economic_identity: Democratic socialism with public ownership, independent labour, universal education, and gradual enterprise reform.

parties.name: National United Party
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The National United Party was founded underground in Yerevan on 24 April 1966, the anniversary of the genocide, by the painter Haykaz Khachatryan, Stepan Zatikyan and Shahen Harutyunyan. Its founders were arrested in 1968, and the student Paruyr Hayrikyan, who took over the leadership, was seized by the KGB in March 1969. On 1 January 1970 it survives as a few cells of young workers and students while its leaders sit in prison.

Its programme, 'For the Nation and the Homeland', demands an independent and democratic Armenia, redress for the genocide and the reunification of the Armenian lands held by Turkey and Azerbaijan. It spreads leaflets, honours the martyrs of 1915 and treats Russian rule and Turkish denial as twin enemies. Its leverage is moral rather than material: the nationalist mood of Armenian youth since the rallies of 1965.

parties.name: Communist Party of Azerbaijan
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Communist Party of Azerbaijan is the republican branch of the CPSU and the only legal party in the Azerbaijan SSR. In July 1969 Moscow replaced the long-serving Veli Akhundov with Heydar Aliyev, the 46-year-old chairman of the republic's KGB, as First Secretary.

Aliyev has opened a loud campaign against corruption, bribery and the sale of posts, purging Akhundov's appointees and placing trusted colleagues in key jobs. The party promotes oil, cotton, viticulture and industrial growth, Soviet patriotism and a carefully controlled Azerbaijani identity. Its power rests on the nomenklatura, the security organs and Aliyev's rapidly growing standing with Leonid Brezhnev.
parties.economic_identity: Public oil refining and engineering paired with a choice between export rents and wider non-oil industry.

parties.name: Müsavat Party
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Müsavat Party, founded in Baku in 1911, led the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic until the Red Army's invasion of April 1920. Destroyed at home, it survives in Turkish exile as a small émigré party carrying the legacy of its leader Mammad Amin Rasulzade, who died in Ankara in 1955.

Its programme is national democracy: an independent, secular Azerbaijani republic with a parliament, private property and close ties to Turkey and the West. Inside the Soviet republic the name Müsavat is a political curse, invoked by propaganda against 'bourgeois nationalists'. Its leverage lies in family memories of 1918, in Turkey's protection and in the slow rediscovery of national history among Baku students.
parties.economic_identity: Secular parliamentary nationalism, private trade, civic citizenship, and oil wealth used for broad public development.

parties.name: Union of Writers of Azerbaijan
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
The Union of Writers of Azerbaijan is the official association of the republic's authors and the most prestigious forum of the Azerbaijani intelligentsia. Beside senior figures such as the novelist Mirza Ibrahimov stand poets and prose writers like Rasul Rza, Bakhtiyar Vahabzade, Anar and Elchin, whose works test the limits of censorship with modernist forms and national themes.

The writers press for wider use of Azerbaijani in schools and offices, freer debate on history and gentler censorship, while proclaiming loyalty to Soviet power. Vahabzade's poem Gülüstan, lamenting the 1813 treaty that divided Azerbaijan, earned him party reprimands. Their leverage lies in a mass readership and the party's need for respected national voices.
parties.economic_identity: Secular cultural renewal, university autonomy, local publishing, and a diversified service economy.

parties.name: Azerbaijan Trade Union Council
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
The Azerbaijan Trade Union Council is the republican body of the Soviet trade unions, organising Baku's oil workers, refinery hands, textile operatives and builders. It inherits the memory of the great Baku oil strikes of 1904 and 1914 and officially serves as a 'school of communism' under party supervision.

Within its committees a pragmatic, welfare-minded current presses for housing, wages, pensions and safety on the ageing Absheron oilfields and the offshore platforms of Neft Daşları. It favours consultation with workers over mobilisation campaigns and fair distribution over prestige projects. Its leverage lies in the oil workers, whose output the Union still needs, and in control of sanatoriums, holidays and housing queues.
parties.economic_identity: Labour-led reform, collective bargaining, public ownership of energy, and worker participation in industrial conversion.

parties.name: Communist Party of Kazakhstan
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Communist Party of Kazakhstan is the republican branch of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union and the sole legal party of the Kazakh SSR. Since December 1964 it has been led by First Secretary Dinmukhamed Kunaev, a mining engineer, close ally of Leonid Brezhnev and candidate member of the Soviet Politburo.

The party carries out Moscow's plan for grain, coal, metals and the space programme while quietly widening the room for Kazakh cadres. It is loyal to the USSR and hostile to Washington and Beijing alike after the 1969 border clashes. Its power rests on the nomenklatura, the obkom secretaries of every province and Kunaev's personal line to Brezhnev.
parties.economic_identity: Public mining and grain production balanced against regional infrastructure, water protection, and household services.

parties.name: Spirit of Alash
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
The Spirit of Alash is the quiet heritage of the Alash Orda, the liberal Kazakh autonomy of 1917-1920 led by Alikhan Bukeikhanov, Akhmet Baitursynov and Mirzhakyp Dulatov, all of whom died in Stalin's purges. Their names are still banned in 1970, but philologists, historians and older teachers in Alma-Ata pass on their writings in private.

The circle dreams of constitutional rule, a Kazakh parliament, freedom of the press and an end to Russification, much as Bukeikhanov's Kadet allies once did. It looks with sympathy towards Western democracy but avoids open dissent. Its leverage lies in the universities, the Academy of Sciences and the Kazakh-language press, where every rehabilitation debate reopens the question of Alash.
parties.economic_identity: Constitutional national autonomy, civic citizenship, education, agrarian modernization, and private enterprise under law.

parties.name: Earth, Bow to Man!
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
Earth, Bow to Man! takes its name from the 1961 poem with which Olzhas Suleimenov greeted Gagarin's flight from Baikonur. In 1970 Suleimenov is the star of a young, bilingual Kazakh intelligentsia of poets, film-makers and journalists who grew up in the Thaw and still believe that socialism can be humane and creative.

They want less censorship, more respect for the Kazakh language and history, honest discussion of the famine of the 1930s and a Communist Party that listens rather than commands. They do not challenge Soviet power or the Warsaw Pact. Their strength lies in culture: theatre premieres, literary journals, Kazakhfilm and the admiration of urban students.
parties.economic_identity: Humanist public health, scientific knowledge, local oversight, and safer industrial development rooted in Kazakhstan’s 1960s civic institutions.

parties.name: Kazakh Land
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
Kazakh Land is the populist mood born in 1960-1961, when Zhumabek Tashenev, then chairman of the Kazakh Council of Ministers, refused Khrushchev's demand to hand the northern Virgin Lands provinces to Russia and was sacked for it. In 1970 Tashenev is a demoted provincial official, but his stand is told in every Kazakh village.

The current speaks for rural Kazakhs who feel outnumbered by Slavic settlers: the land must stay Kazakh, jobs and flats should go to locals, and Moscow's projects must not swallow pasture and graves. It distrusts both Russian officials and Western ideas. Its leverage is resentment, the village elders and the youth of the south.
parties.economic_identity: Land stewardship, regional representation, rural services, and diversified employment beyond extraction settlements.

parties.name: Communist Party of Uzbekistan
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Communist Party of Uzbekistan is the republican branch of the CPSU and the only legal party in the Uzbek SSR. Since 1959 it has been led by First Secretary Sharof Rashidov, a writer from Jizzakh and candidate member of the Politburo, who has made himself the indispensable broker between Moscow and the most populous republic of Central Asia.

The party preaches loyalty to Brezhnev and the friendship of peoples, while Rashidov presents Tashkent as the Soviet showcase to Asia and Africa. Its overriding task is cotton, the ‘white gold’ delivered in ever larger plans, alongside the rebuilding of Tashkent after the 1966 earthquake. Its power is total, resting on every appointment and on Rashidov's network of loyal regional clans.
parties.economic_identity: State cotton and textile production with a choice between export specialization, food crops, and water-saving industry.

parties.name: Writers' Union of Uzbekistan
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
The Writers' Union of Uzbekistan is the republic's official literary institution and one of the most prestigious in Central Asia. First Secretary Sharof Rashidov, himself a novelist, once chaired it, and its ranks include the poetess Zulfiya, the playwright Komil Yashin and a generation of younger poets who fill the journals and publishing houses of Tashkent.

Beneath the official optimism it nurtures a cultural conservatism: reverence for Alisher Navoi and the classical heritage, defence of the Uzbek language and a respectful image of family, mahalla and village. It accepts Soviet power and Moscow's leadership but quietly resists Russification. Its leverage is prestige and the patronage of Rashidov, who protects writers who serve the republic's image.
parties.economic_identity: Cultural self-government, language education, publishing, and technical investment in food processing and irrigation.

parties.name: New Jadids
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
The New Jadids are a loose circle of young Uzbek poets, historians and teachers in Tashkent and Samarkand who see themselves as heirs of the Jadid reformers of the early century, Behbudiy, Fitrat and Cho'lpon, whose works remain largely unpublished. The patriotic and searching verse of poets such as Erkin Vohidov and Abdulla Oripov gives the mood its voice.

They want liberal reform within the Soviet system: freer expression, an honest history of Turkestan, modern education, the rule of law and an end to the cotton monoculture's grip on people's lives. They admire Western learning but are no émigré agents. Their leverage is moral and cultural, felt in universities, editorial boards and the kitchens of the Tashkent intelligentsia.
parties.economic_identity: Modernist education, technical schools, constitutional administration, and gradual diversification from cotton.

parties.name: Women's Councils of Uzbekistan
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
The Women's Councils of Uzbekistan are the network of party-sponsored women's committees attached to factories, kolkhozes and local soviets, heirs of the Hujum unveiling campaign launched in 1927. Their most prominent patron is Yodgor Nasriddinova, Chairwoman of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet and the highest-ranking woman in Central Asian politics.

They push a social-democratic agenda inside the Soviet framework: schooling and careers for girls, creches and maternity care, the fight against child marriage, polygamy and bride-price, and relief for women worn down in the cotton fields. Loyal to Moscow, they put pressure on local patriarchs and mullahs. Their leverage lies in the regime's need to show the world an emancipated Soviet East.
parties.economic_identity: Women's civic representation, rural health and education, food processing, and access to paid technical work.

parties.name: Mahalla Elders
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
The Mahalla Elders are the white-bearded aksakals who preside over the neighbourhoods of Uzbek towns and the quarters of its villages. Officially their mahalla committees are a minor tier of local administration, but in practice they settle disputes, organise weddings, circumcisions and funerals, direct hashar communal labour and decide whose family is respectable.

They guard a non-ideological conservatism: respect for elders, family honour, modest dress, hospitality and quiet piety, accommodating Soviet power as long as it leaves the household alone. They care little for Washington or Moscow and a great deal for the street. Their leverage is social control: in the mahalla nobody marries, builds or prospers without their blessing.
parties.economic_identity: Local mediation, community credit, irrigation rules, and a secular civic settlement with strong municipal accountability.

parties.name: Communist Party of Turkmenistan
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Communist Party of Turkmenistan is the republican branch of the CPSU and the only legal party in the Turkmen SSR. In December 1969 Muhammetnazar Gapurov, until then chairman of the republic's Council of Ministers, replaced Balysh Ovezov as First Secretary, and he is now installing his own cadres in Ashgabat and the district committees.

The party follows Brezhnev's line of stability and cadre security and pledges unconditional loyalty to Moscow. Its priorities are cotton, the extension of the Karakum Canal and the exploitation of newly discovered gas fields in the desert. Its power is total: it appoints every director, editor and kolkhoz chairman, and its patronage reaches deep into the tribal networks of the Ahal, Mary, Çärjew and Daşhowuz oases.
parties.economic_identity: State gas and cotton production balanced against water conservation, local processing, and costly transport links.

parties.name: Union of Writers of the Turkmen SSR
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
The Union of Writers of the Turkmen SSR is the republic's official literary body and the guardian of its printed language. Its patriarch is Berdi Kerbabaýew, author of the revolutionary novel ‘Aýgytly ädim’ and of ‘Nebitdag’, and around him gather the poets, novelists and critics who fill Ashgabat's journals and publishing houses.

Loyal to Moscow on paper, the union nurses a cautious cultural conservatism: it defends Turkmen against creeping Russian in schools and offices, champions the classical poet Magtymguly and the Görogly epic, and resists attempts to erase the pre-revolutionary heritage. It has no ministries and no guns, but it shapes how Turkmens see themselves, and the party needs its pens.
parties.economic_identity: Turkmen-language education, cultural publishing, technical training, and carefully negotiated local development.

parties.name: Turkmenfilm New Wave
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
The young directors and cameramen of the Turkmenfilm studio in Ashgabat have become the boldest artistic voice in the republic. Bulat Mansurov's ‘The Contest’ and ‘Quenching the Thirst’, adapted from Yuri Trifonov's novel about the builders of the Karakum Canal, and the striking camerawork of Khodjakuli Narliev have won Turkmen cinema attention far beyond Central Asia.

The circle stands for artistic freedom and honest portrayals of village life, old customs and the human cost of Soviet modernisation. It is not anti-Soviet, yet its films test the limits of censorship, and its members admire Italian and French cinema. Its leverage is prestige: festival prizes and all-Union acclaim make it hard for Ashgabat's ideologists to silence.
parties.economic_identity: Cultural industry, vocational education, public debate, and urban services alongside rural water investment.

parties.name: Turkmen Republican Council of Trade Unions
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
The Turkmen Republican Council of Trade Unions organises the oilmen of Nebitdag and Çeleken, the textile workers of Ashgabat, the dockers of Krasnovodsk and the hundreds of thousands employed on state farms and construction sites. Like every Soviet union body it answers to the party, administering social insurance, sanatoria, housing queues and holiday vouchers rather than leading strikes.

Within those limits it voices a cautious social reformism: higher wages and shorter shifts in the scorching summer, better housing in the canal settlements, more consumer goods and the bonuses promised by the Kosygin reforms. Its strength lies in sheer membership and control of welfare funds, which make it the regime's main channel to the working class.
parties.economic_identity: Worker bargaining, public housing, safer extraction, and negotiated restructuring of state industries.

parties.name: Council of Elders
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
The Council of Elders is the informal authority of the white-bearded ýaşulular who still lead the Teke, Ýomut, Ärsary, Salyr and Saryk tribes behind the façade of the collective farms. Collectivisation broke their herds and holdings, yet tribe and lineage still decide marriages, disputes, water shares and even who becomes kolkhoz chairman or district secretary.

They are conservatives of a quiet, rural kind: they defend bride-price, family honour, customary law and the authority of age, and distrust Russian newcomers and urban radicals alike. Neither pro-Western nor truly Soviet, they know how to live with whoever controls the canals. Their leverage is the village itself, which no outsider can govern without their consent.
parties.economic_identity: Local mediation, water stewardship, pasture access, and municipal consent over gas and cotton development.

parties.name: Communist Party of Kirghizia
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Communist Party of Kirghizia is the republican branch of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union and the only legal party of the Kirghiz SSR. Since 1961 it has been led by First Secretary Turdakun Usubaliyev, an energetic and loyal Brezhnev-era leader who never misses a chance to praise Moscow.

The party drives industrialisation, the Toktogul hydropower scheme, sheep breeding and the education of a Kyrgyz professional class, while firmly suppressing anything that smells of nationalism. It backs the USSR against both the United States and China across the Tian Shan. Its power rests on the nomenklatura, the obkoms of Osh, Naryn and Issyk-Kul, and Usubaliyev's standing in Moscow.
parties.economic_identity: Public hydropower, regional workshops, livestock processing, and equal access across a mountainous republic.

parties.name: Defenders of Manas
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
The Defenders of Manas are the scholars, teachers and epic singers who rescued the Manas epic after it was denounced as feudal in 1952. Their living symbol in 1970 is the great manaschi Sayakbay Karalaev, whose recitations fill concert halls and whose versions are being recorded by the Academy of Sciences.

They stand for continuity: the epic, the clan genealogy, respect for elders and the Kyrgyz language as the soul of the nation. They avoid open politics and accept Soviet power, but distrust Russification and the uprooting of nomadic culture. Their leverage is moral authority over a people for whom Manas is still scripture, history and law combined.
parties.economic_identity: Cultural education, multilingual civic institutions, mountain services, and community-led preservation of oral traditions.

parties.name: The White Ship
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
The White Ship is the circle of writers, film-makers and young scholars around Chingiz Aitmatov, the Lenin Prize laureate whose novella of that name appears in the Moscow journal Novy Mir in 1970. They are the Kyrgyz face of the Thaw, admired across the Union and protected by Aitmatov's fame.

They stand for conscience over dogma: freedom of artistic expression, truth about the past, protection of nature and of national memory against careerist officials. They remain inside the Soviet system and avoid any link to the West. Their leverage is prestige: Aitmatov's books sell in millions, his films are seen everywhere and even the Central Committee hesitates to attack him.
parties.economic_identity: Environmental education, local services, public accountability, and low-impact rural and cultural employment.

parties.name: Kosygin Reformers
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
The Kosygin Reformers are economists, planners and enterprise directors in Frunze who embraced the economic reform launched by Alexei Kosygin in 1965, with its enterprise autonomy, profit indicators and material incentives. By 1970 the reform is stalling in Moscow, but its supporters still run factories and departments of the Kirghiz Gosplan.

They want managers freed from petty planning, wages tied to productivity, consumer goods for workers and more investment in light industry and services. They remain loyal socialists and support the USSR's foreign line, but admire Hungarian and Yugoslav experiments. Their leverage lies in measurable results and in allies within the State Planning Committee in Moscow.
parties.economic_identity: Reform socialism, enterprise accounting, manager responsibility, and regional investment within a public economy.

parties.name: The South
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
The South is the bloc of kolkhoz chairmen, district officials and village elders of Osh and Jalal-Abad provinces, the populous, cotton-growing half of the republic that feels shut out of power by northerners in Frunze. Kyrgyz and Uzbek notables there share a world of bazaars, mosques, lineages and patronage.

They defend traditional family life, respect for elders and a fair share of posts and investment for the south. They are loyal to Soviet rule in form but govern by custom in practice, and have no interest in foreign blocs. Their leverage is numbers, the cotton harvest and the ability to deliver or withhold the south's cooperation.
parties.economic_identity: Regional representation, irrigation, farm-to-market access, and balanced public investment across north and south.

profile.name: Tajik SSR
profile.context: Irrigated cotton, hydropower and regional inequalities

regional.name: Uneven Regional Investment
regional.description: The republic's established economy rests on irrigated cotton, hydropower and regional inequalities. These strengths bring inherited costs in transport, public administration and the inputs needed to keep production operating reliably.

parties.name: Communist Party of Tajikistan
parties.status: Existing party, exile body or underground organisation
parties.description:
The Communist Party of Tajikistan is the republican branch of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union and the only legal party of the Tajik SSR. Since 1961 it has been led by First Secretary Jabbor Rasulov, an agronomist from the Leninabad region and a cautious, dependable ally of Leonid Brezhnev.

The party drives cotton production, the construction of the Nurek dam and the education of a Tajik professional class, while balancing the rival regions of the republic. It is loyal to Moscow, hostile to the United States and wary of China and of religious revival across the Afghan border. Its power rests on the nomenklatura and the Leninabad cadres around Rasulov.
parties.economic_identity: Public cotton and hydropower with food security, local industry, and a stronger share of investment for mountain districts.

parties.name: Samanid Heritage
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
The Samanid Heritage school unites historians, orientalists and teachers around Bobojon Ghafurov, former First Secretary of the republic and since 1956 director of the Institute of Oriental Studies in Moscow, who is writing a grand history of the Tajiks. They present the Samanid state of the tenth century as the golden age of the nation.

They stand for continuity with the Persian classical tradition, pride in Rudaki and Avicenna, respect for family and learning, and a Tajik identity distinct from the Turkic world. They remain loyal Soviet scholars and avoid confrontation. Their leverage is Ghafurov's prestige in Moscow, the Academy of Sciences and the school curriculum.
parties.economic_identity: Tajik-language education, historical research, civic citizenship, and regional public services.

parties.name: Sixties Generation
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
The Sixties Generation are the young Tajik poets and writers of the Thaw, among them Loiq Sherali and Bozor Sobir, who broke with the stiff verse of socialist realism and returned to the language of Hafez and Rumi. In 1970 they publish in Dushanbe journals, read before packed halls and are watched warily by the censors.

They want freedom of expression, honest treatment of the past, the restoration of Persian as a living literary language and a culture open to the wider Persian world. They avoid open dissent and any link to the West. Their leverage is the enormous popularity of poetry and the admiration of students across the republic.
parties.economic_identity: Literary civic reform, public education, open research, and provincial investment rather than a single nationalist programme.

parties.name: Tajik Republican Council of Trade Unions
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
The Tajik Republican Council of Trade Unions is the republican branch of the All-Union Central Council of Trade Unions, organising textile workers, miners, builders and state-farm labourers from Leninabad to Kurgan-Tyube. In 1970 it remains a transmission belt of the party, but it distributes housing, holidays and social insurance to hundreds of thousands.

Within those limits it presses for better wages, safer workplaces, kindergartens and housing in the fast-growing towns, and for a fair share of jobs for Tajiks in industry. It supports the Soviet order and its foreign policy. Its leverage lies in the factory committees and in the welfare network on which workers' families depend.
parties.economic_identity: Labour bargaining, public services, workplace safety, and measured restructuring of state enterprises.

parties.name: Nuri's Circle
parties.status: Alternate-history governing coalition drawn from the registered 1970 institution or circle
parties.description:
Nuri's Circle gathers young believers around Said Abdullo Nuri, a twenty-two-year-old from a Karategin family resettled in the Vakhsh valley, who studies religion privately with underground teachers including Muhammadjan Hindustani. On 1 January 1970 it is an informal group of friends who meet to study, pray and discuss the state of Muslims.

They want Islam restored to public life through education, preaching and moral renewal rather than violence, and dream of a society where faith and modern learning go together. They oppose Soviet atheism but are wary of foreign powers. Their leverage is youthful energy, kinship networks among the Gharmi resettlers and the hunger for religious knowledge.
parties.economic_identity: Civic religious renewal, lawful education, local charity, equal citizenship, and a cautious path from underground networks to accountable public service.

groups.title: The Republican Administration
groups.note: The First Secretary is the political leader in January 1970. If the Union or republic changes its political system, the shared programme continues under its actual republican leadership.

Its specialised institutions now possess skills and capacity that would be difficult to assemble in isolation, together with a lasting dependence on the customers, suppliers and common standards that made their growth possible. Historical precedent: Kazakh grain, Uzbek cotton, and Moldovan grapes and fruit illustrate the Union's regional crop specializations.

nodes.title: Civilian Industry
nodes.description: Tractors, machinery, electrical goods and consumer products give a republic a place in everyday economic life across the Union. A civilian industrial programme can broaden skilled employment and commercial capacity, while requiring dependable energy and a large market for its output. Historical precedent: Minsk's tractor works and Chisinau's T-50B vineyard-tractor plant show civilian machinery production serving different farm economies.
